Why it's harder to hear sounds that are coming from water despite sound having much higher speed in water?

Clarifications:

Are you asking why they sound weird if two buddies stick their heads in a pool and try to talk? Or if somebody is underwater and trying to talk to somebody on the surface or vice versa?

Ok, so, the people here are kind of hitting on the answer and kinda not.

When we attempt to talk underwater, the energy in the vibrations of air do not transmit to water very well. It's not that we can't hear it, it just doesn't like to transfer from one medium to another. It's finicky that way.

What does get transferred is distorted and compressed by the density of the water, so you will hear different pitches. This is evidenced by some super fantastic speakers designed for pools. They have to adjust the pitch and everything so it will sound like it's supposed to. Pull one out of the water and it sounds like crap.

The same answer will hold true for most scenarios you can imagine where one person is using non mechanical means to communicate with somebody underwater. Energy doesn't like transferring, so most of it will just spread out along the surface of the water. This is why you can barely hear somebody when you're underwater, but can hear a pin drop from 30 yards away. Water is just fantastic at transferring sounds, but we lack the proper adapters to use it naturally.
I think they short answer would be that the human ear is designed to detect fluctuations in air currents. And since water is significantly thicker than air, we have trouble.

This is just a theory, but when you listen to people talk under water, the sound is being converted from air to water and then back to air before hearing it. If you had vocal cords and ear drums that were designed to work submersed in water, it would probably sound much more clear, but I'm not sure what it would sound like.

Mostly what others have touched on. When sound is created in air it is really a compression wave. Your eardrum vibrates in response to that wave, at frequencies that are the same/similar to those that produced it. In water though, the fluid can't compress so the waves, and therefore the frequencies, get distorted to something unintelligible. If our vocal chords and ears had evolved for hearing in water, sounds in air would probably sound super high pitched and distorted.
